Photo: Oleg/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: levels of toxic forever chemicals in English rivers fall dramatically since 2016, a bioengineered chewing gum fights microbes linked to head and neck cancers, and the Italian region of Calabria offers free village homes for ten years to attract new residents.

Huge drop in levels of toxic forever chemicals in English rivers since 2016
The decline in the chemicals known as PFOS and PFOA has largely been attributed to stricter restrictions on their use in products, after increasing evidence pointed to their damaging impact on human health. New data show that concentrations in English rivers have fallen by 30% and 29% respectively, and levels in freshwater fish have fallen 49%.

Source: BBC News

Bioengineered chewing gum reduces HPV levels by up to 93%
The cancer-fighting gum eliminates two harmful bacterial species linked to head and neck cancers, with oral samples from cancer patients show a huge drop in HPV levels after a single dose. The treatment also spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

Source: Science Daily

Stronger flu shot associated with 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
Researchers at UTHealth Houston analysed data from nearly 200,000 adults aged 65 and older and found that those who received the high-dose flu vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of Alzheimer’s compared with unvaccinated individuals. This represents a greater reduction than the approximately 40% previously associated with the standard-dose flu vaccine.

Source: Science Daily

Court strikes down Trinidad and Tobago law criminalising gay sex

A London-based court has overturned a law in Trinidad and Tobago that criminalised consensual same-sex relations between men in the Caribbean nation. The ruling was issued by the country’s final court of appeal, which remains based in the UK as a legacy of its colonial past.

Source: Deutsche Welle

Community dialogue cuts child marriage by 64% in Vietnam's Lang Son province
The drop of 64% in cases between 2021 and 2025, alongside the elimination of consanguineous marriages, is largely attributed to community-based dialogue campaigns conducted in Tay, Nung and Dao languages, bringing local women’s groups, village elders and community officials together to educate families about the health, social and educational consequences of early marriage.

Source: Vietnam Law Magazine
